slides.0.title: Course Introduction
slides.0.content:
Congratulations — you are about to complete all the learning in Bordeaux Wine Introduction (L1)! Across the preceding seven lessons, we set out from geography and explored climate, grape varieties, Left Bank vs Right Bank differences, wine types, the AOC system, and tasting techniques. Now it is time to integrate this knowledge and build a complete framework of Bordeaux wine understanding.

This lesson is the summary and assessment course for Level 1. We will systematically review the key points of the seven core topics, trace the logical connections between them, summarise the defining characteristics and strengths of Bordeaux wine, and assess your learning through a comprehensive test. Most importantly, we will map out a pathway for further study, helping you make a smooth transition to Level 2 (in-depth appellation exploration).

Learning Objectives

📚 Systematically Review the L1 Knowledge Framework

Integrate the core content of the six modules: geography, climate, varieties, appellations, classification, and tasting

🔗 Build a Knowledge Network

Understand the causal logic and interplay between soil, climate, variety, and style

🎯 Assess Learning Outcomes

Use a comprehensive test to gauge how well you have mastered the material and identify areas needing reinforcement

🌟 Summarise Core Characteristics

Distil the unique strengths of Bordeaux wine and the key factors behind its world-class standing

🚀 Plan an Advanced Learning Pathway

Learn what Level 2 covers and set clear goals for the next stage of study

After completing this lesson, you will have a solid foundation in Bordeaux wine knowledge, the capability to move to advanced study, and the confidence to share your understanding of Bordeaux with others. Let us complete this important milestone together!

slides.1.highlights.0.title: Systematic Framework

slides.1.highlights.1.title: Core Points
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Master the most important foundational concepts and characteristics
slides.1.content:
Over the course of seven lessons, we have built a foundational knowledge base for Bordeaux wine. Let us now systematically review these key concepts.

🗺️ Geographic Foundation (L1-1)

Core Concepts
  • Location: South-western France, Atlantic coast
  • River system: The Gironde, Dordogne, and Garonne
  • Left/Right Bank division: Appellation boundaries defined by river geography
  • Regional importance: The world's largest premium wine-producing region
Practical Application
  • Locate Bordeaux on a map
  • Understand the concept of Left and Right Banks
  • Recognise the influence of major rivers on the appellations
  • Appreciate Bordeaux's standing in the French wine industry

🌤️ Climate and Environment (L1-2)

Core Concepts
  • Maritime climate: Characteristics of a temperate maritime climate
  • River moderation: The moderating effect of water bodies on temperature and humidity
  • Four seasons: Seasonal influence on the vine growth cycle
  • Mesoclimates: Climatic differences between sub-regions
Practical Application
  • Understand climate's impact on grape quality
  • Recognise the protective role of the river system
  • Grasp the basic principles of vintage variation
  • Appreciate Bordeaux's unique climatic advantages

🍇 Grape Varieties (L1-3)

Core Concepts
  • Three key red varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc
  • Key white varieties: Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon, Muscadelle
  • The art of blending: Complementarity and balance between varieties
  • Terroir adaptation: Different varieties' suitability to soils and climates
Practical Application
  • Identify the basic characteristics of each variety
  • Understand the fundamental principles of blending
  • Know the correspondence between variety and appellation
  • Recognise how varieties shape a wine's style

⚖️ Left Bank vs Right Bank (L1-4)

Core Concepts
  • Soil differences: Left Bank gravel vs Right Bank clay
  • Variety preference: Left Bank Cabernet vs Right Bank Merlot
  • Style contrast: Power and structure vs elegance and roundness
  • Ageing character: Structure-led vs balance-led development
Practical Application
  • Distinguish the basic characteristics of Left and Right Bank wines
  • Understand how soil influences variety selection
  • Know the key tasting focus points for different styles
  • Choose appropriate pairing and collecting strategies

🍷 Wine Types (L1-5)

Core Concepts
  • Red wine dominance: 85% of production; diverse styles
  • Fine white wines: High-quality dry and sweet expressions
  • Speciality wines: Sparkling, rosé, and Clairet
  • Quality tiers: A complete spectrum from everyday to top-tier
Practical Application
  • Identify the characteristics of different wine types
  • Understand production proportions and market positioning
  • Know the appropriate occasions for each wine type
  • Select wine types that suit your needs

📜 AOC Classification (L1-6)

Core Concepts
  • AOC system: The hierarchy from regional to communal level
  • 1855 Classification: The historic Left Bank classification system
  • Right Bank classification: The dynamic Saint-Émilion system
  • Other systems: Graves Classification, Cru Bourgeois, etc.
Practical Application
  • Understand the significance and limitations of classification systems
  • Identify the quality characteristics of different levels
  • Understand the relationship between classification and price
  • Select quality levels that suit your budget

👃 Tasting Fundamentals (L1-7)

Core Concepts
  • Tasting preparation: The importance of environment, equipment, and temperature
  • Visual evaluation: Colour, clarity, and viscosity observation
  • Olfactory analysis: Identification and analysis of the three aroma tiers
  • Methods and techniques: A systematic approach to evaluation
Practical Application
  • Correctly prepare a tasting environment
  • Master basic observation techniques
  • Identify the main aroma types
  • Build a systematic tasting habit
slides.1.quiz.question: Which is the correct pairing of the dominant Left Bank variety with its soil type?
slides.1.quiz.explanation: Bordeaux's Left Bank is dominated by Cabernet Sauvignon, growing predominantly on gravel soils. This combination is what gives Left Bank wines their powerful structure and excellent ageing potential.
slides.3.title: Comprehensive Ability Assessment
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Knowledge Test
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Evaluate learning outcomes through a variety of question types
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Practical Application
slides.3.content:
Through a comprehensive, multi-format test, gain a full assessment of your grasp of Bordeaux wine fundamentals and your ability to apply them in practice.

📚 Fundamental Knowledge Test

Geography and Climate (25%)
  • Location: Bordeaux's position in France; the principal rivers
  • Left/Right Bank division: Geographic concept and appellation distribution
  • Climate characteristics: Traits and influences of the maritime climate
  • Seasonal change: The impact of four seasons on vine growth

Sample questions:

1. In which part of France is Bordeaux located?

2. How are the Left and Right Banks defined?

3. What role does the river system play in Bordeaux's climate?

Varieties and Blending (25%)
  • Variety identification: The characteristics of the main red and white varieties
  • Blending principles: The role and proportion of different varieties
  • Terroir adaptation: The match between variety and soil/climate
  • Style influence: How variety shapes wine style

Sample questions:

1. What are the main characteristics of Merlot?

2. Which variety dominates the Left Bank, and which the Right?

3. Which varieties make up Bordeaux white wine?

Classification Systems (25%)
  • AOC system: The principles of the appellation system
  • 1855 Classification: Structure of the historic Left Bank ranking
  • Right Bank classification: Characteristics of the Saint-Émilion system
  • Other systems: Graves Classification, Cru Bourgeois, etc.

Sample questions:

1. How many tiers are there in the 1855 Classification?

2. What is distinctive about the Saint-Émilion Classification?

3. What is the core function of the AOC system?

Tasting Application (25%)
  • Tasting preparation: Environment, temperature, equipment
  • Observation techniques: Colour and clarity analysis
  • Aroma identification: Classification of the three aroma tiers
  • Tasting method: Systematic evaluation process

Sample questions:

1. What is the appropriate tasting temperature for young red wine?

2. Which variety is typically associated with the pencil shavings aroma?

3. What does an orange rim typically indicate?

🎭 Real-World Application Scenarios

Scenario 1: Wine Selection

Situation: A customer wants a Bordeaux red suitable for long-term cellaring

  • Budget: 500–1,000 CNY
  • Goal: Enjoy after 5–10 years of cellaring
  • Preference: Favours structured wines
  • Occasion: A special anniversary

Recommended approach:

  • Choose a Left Bank appellation (powerful structure)
  • Prioritise communal-level AOCs
  • Look for wines with a high Cabernet Sauvignon proportion
  • Select wines with some bottle age already
Scenario 2: Food Pairing

Situation: Selecting a Bordeaux wine for a steak set menu at a French restaurant

  • Main: Pan-seared steak with red wine sauce
  • Sides: Roasted vegetables and mashed potato
  • Guest profile: Business dinner
  • Budget: Mid-range

Pairing logic:

  • Steak calls for a red wine with generous tannins
  • Left Bank wines are better suited to rich, full-flavoured meat dishes
  • Choose Médoc or a specific communal AOC
  • Avoid wines that are too young or too old
Scenario 3: Vintage Assessment

Situation: Evaluating the character and investment value of different Bordeaux vintages

  • Climate: Weather conditions of the vintage year
  • Scores: Ratings from authoritative organisations
  • Market: Price trends
  • Drinking window: The optimal time to enjoy

Assessment criteria:

  • Understand the impact of vintage on quality
  • Analyse the relationship between climate and wine style
  • Assess ageing potential and investment value
  • Formulate a sensible purchasing and consumption plan

📊 Assessment Criteria

Grade Levels
Excellent (90–100)
  • Comprehensive grasp of foundational knowledge
  • Able to apply knowledge flexibly to real-world scenarios
  • Capable of independent analysis and judgment
  • Ready to proceed to Level 2 Intermediate
Good (80–89)
  • Essentially masters core concepts
  • Can handle common practical scenarios
  • Some knowledge points need reinforcement
  • Recommended to review before proceeding to Level 2
Pass (70–79)
  • Grasps the basic knowledge framework
  • Can understand foundational concepts
  • Practical application ability needs strengthening
  • Recommended to revisit some lessons
Needs Improvement (60–69)
  • Significant gaps in foundational knowledge
  • Application ability needs substantial improvement
  • Recommended to retake the Level 1 course
  • Strengthen understanding of core concepts
slides.3.quiz.question: Taking into account the characteristics of Left Bank wines, which situation is best suited to a Left Bank choice?
slides.3.quiz.options.0: Casual enjoyment at a summer gathering
slides.3.quiz.explanation: Left Bank wines are dominated by Cabernet Sauvignon, giving them powerful structure, generous tannins, and excellent ageing potential. They are best suited to long-term cellaring and investment, developing greater complexity as they mature over time.
slides.4.title: Advanced Learning Plan and Recommendations
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Learning Pathway
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Develop a personalised Bordeaux study advancement plan
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Skill Development
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Methods for continuously improving tasting and application abilities
slides.4.content:
Having completed the Level 1 foundational course, establish a clear advanced learning pathway to deepen your understanding and tasting ability for Bordeaux wine.

🚀 Immediate Next Steps

Practical Tasting Practice
  • Entry-level wines: Purchase 2–3 basic Bordeaux AOC wines from different appellations
  • Comparative tasting: Left Bank vs Right Bank entry-level comparison
  • Variety identification: Taste wines dominated by a single variety
  • Vintage comparison: Compare different vintages from the same château
  • Record keeping: Build a systematic tasting-notes habit
Knowledge Application in Practice
  • Wine list analysis: Analyse Bordeaux selections at restaurants or wine merchants
  • Price research: Understand the price ranges for different classification levels
  • Vintage study: Research the characteristics of classic recent vintages
  • Appellation exploration: Delve deeper into a specific appellation of interest
  • Pairing experiments: Try different food and wine combination

📚 Preparing for the Level 2 Intermediate Course

Confirming Prerequisite Mastery
  • Geography: Able to accurately identify major appellation locations
  • Varieties: Familiar with the characteristics of the six principal varieties
  • Classification: Understands the significance of different classification systems
  • Tasting: Can conduct a basic sensory evaluation
  • Terminology: Uses basic wine vocabulary correctly
Level 2 Course Preview
  • In-depth appellations: Detailed study of each communal AOC's character
  • Château studies: Deep dive into the history and style of key estates
  • Vintage analysis: Learn vintage assessment and investment strategy
  • Advanced tasting: Master professional tasting techniques and vocabulary
  • Collecting and investment: Bordeaux wine collecting and investment guide

🎯 Skill Development Recommendations

Sensory Training
  • Aroma training: Practise using aroma kits or the Wine Aroma Wheel
  • Variety comparison: Simultaneously taste wines dominated by different varieties
  • Blind tasting: Gradually attempt blind tasting without label information
  • Building memory: Develop a personal sensory memory library
  • Descriptive ability: Improve the precision of aroma and palate descriptions
Analytical Ability
  • Appellation analysis: Learn to infer appellation from flavour profile
  • Vintage estimation: Deduce approximate vintage from wine character
  • Quality evaluation: Objectively assess a wine's quality level
  • Value assessment: Evaluate a wine's quality-to-price ratio
  • Pairing thinking: Develop logical thinking about food and wine pairing
Communication and Expression
  • Professional vocabulary: Use wine terminology accurately
  • Recommendation skills: Recommend suitable wines based on client needs
  • Teaching and sharing: Share Bordeaux knowledge with others
  • Written records: Write tasting notes and commentary
  • Cultural understanding: Appreciate Bordeaux's cultural background

🏆 Long-Term Learning Goals

Enthusiast Pathway
  • Personal collection: Build a personal Bordeaux wine cellar
  • Social tasting: Organise or participate in tasting events
  • Travel experience: Plan a trip to Bordeaux wine country
  • Continued learning: Stay updated on regional news and developments
  • Cultural appreciation: Deepen your understanding of French wine culture
Professional Development Pathway
  • Sommelier certification: Pursue an international sommelier qualification
  • Wine industry: Enter the wine trade or hospitality industry
  • Wine education: Become a wine educator
  • Investment advisory: Provide wine investment advice
  • Writing and critique: Become a professional wine critic
Academic Research Pathway
  • In-depth research: Choose a specific appellation or topic to research in depth
  • History and culture: Study Bordeaux's history and cultural heritage
  • Market analysis: Analyse Bordeaux wine market trends
  • Technical innovation: Follow developments in winemaking technology
  • Academic exchange: Attend academic conferences and symposia

📈 Success Indicators

Knowledge Mastery Indicators
  • Accurate identification: Appellation identification accuracy of 80% or above
  • Variety recognition: Able to identify the dominant variety
  • Vintage estimation: Can roughly judge a wine's approximate age
  • Quality assessment: Objectively assess a wine's quality level
  • Value judgment: Fairly evaluate quality-to-price ratio
Application Ability Indicators
  • Wine selection: Choosing appropriate wines for different occasions
  • Pairing skills: Successful food and wine pairing experiences
  • Cellar planning: Formulating a sensible collecting plan
  • Investment decisions: Making informed investment choices
  • Knowledge sharing: Effectively passing on knowledge to others
slides.4.quiz.question: After completing the Level 1 foundational course, what is the most important next learning activity?
slides.4.quiz.options.1: Engage in practical tasting and comparative exercises
slides.4.quiz.explanation: After completing Level 1, the most important step is to practise actual tasting — by tasting wines from different appellations, varieties, and vintages to consolidate theoretical knowledge and build sensory memory.
slides.5.title: Level 1 Complete
slides.5.description: Congratulations on completing all Level 1 lessons! You have built a comprehensive foundation of Bordeaux wine knowledge: from the geographic distinction between Left and Right Banks to varietal blending, from appellation character to classification systems, and from tasting skills to evaluation criteria. You now have a solid base from which to understand and enjoy Bordeaux wine — and you are ready to progress to the more in-depth study of Level 2!

slides.2.componentProps.items.0.question: What is the dominant red grape variety commonly found on the Left Bank (Médoc)?
slides.2.componentProps.items.0.explanat: The Left Bank is known for its gravelly soils that allow Cabernet Sauvignon to ripen fully, producing wines with defined structure and firm tannins.
slides.2.componentProps.items.1.question: What is the typical soil and dominant variety pairing for the Right Bank Saint-Émilion?
slides.2.componentProps.items.1.explanat: Saint-Émilion is dominated by clay and limestone, which favour Merlot, producing wines with a round mouthfeel and ripe fruit flavours.
slides.2.componentProps.items.2.question: Pessac-Léognan AOC belongs to which major region?
slides.2.componentProps.items.2.explanat: Pessac-Léognan is a prestigious sub-appellation within the Graves region, located just south of Bordeaux city.
slides.2.componentProps.items.3.question: The 1855 Classification was primarily for which bank's red wines?
slides.2.componentProps.items.3.explanat: The 1855 Classification covered Left Bank Médoc red wines (plus a separate classification for Sauternes/Barsac sweet whites).
slides.2.componentProps.items.4.question: Which description is commonly used for the Pauillac wine style?
Structured, dark fruit with cedar/pencil shavings
slides.2.componentProps.items.4.explanat: Pauillac is on the Left Bank, where dark fruit, cedar/pencil shavings aromas, and firm tannin structure are typical.
slides.2.componentProps.items.5.question: What type of wine is Entre-Deux-Mers primarily known for?
slides.2.componentProps.items.5.explanat: The Entre-Deux-Mers region is known for fresh, crisp dry whites, typically blends of Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon.
slides.2.componentProps.items.6.question: Which of the following is a classic Bordeaux noble rot sweet white appellation?
slides.2.componentProps.items.6.explanat: Sauternes and Barsac are Bordeaux's renowned noble rot (botrytis) sweet white appellations.
slides.2.componentProps.items.7.question: Compared to other Left Bank villages, Margaux is commonly described as more…
slides.2.componentProps.items.7.explanat: Margaux's style is typified by elegance and refined aromatics, in contrast to the power of Pauillac or Saint-Estèphe.
slides.2.componentProps.items.8.question: What are the typical flavours of Sauvignon Blanc in Bordeaux dry whites?
slides.2.componentProps.items.8.explanat: Sauvignon Blanc typically shows citrus, grass/herb, and mineral notes, complementing Sémillon's body and structure in the blend.
slides.2.componentProps.items.9.question: Which statement best describes the general impression of Left Bank vs. Right Bank?
Left Bank leans towards Merlot; Right Bank towards Cabernet
Left Bank is more structured; Right Bank is rounder
Both banks focus mainly on sweet whites
Both banks focus mainly on rosé
slides.2.componentProps.items.9.explanat: The Left Bank's higher Cabernet proportion produces more structured wines; the Right Bank's higher Merlot creates a rounder, softer mouthfeel.
slides.2.componentProps.items.10.questio: What does an orange rim on a red wine most commonly indicate?
slides.2.componentProps.items.10.explana: An orange rim typically suggests some ageing/development, though this should be assessed alongside other indicators.
slides.2.componentProps.items.11.questio: For pairing with steak and wanting defined tannin support, which is most suitable?
slides.2.componentProps.items.11.explana: For steak, a tannin-rich Left Bank Médoc red is ideal — tannins interact with meat proteins to soften the mouthfeel.
slides.2.componentProps.items.12.questio: Learning vintage performance and investment evaluation is most appropriate as a goal for which stage?
slides.2.componentProps.items.12.explana: Vintage/investment evaluation requires integrating knowledge of appellations, styles, and market dynamics — best built gradually from L2/L3 onwards.
slides.2.componentProps.items.13.questio: Which of the following is most likely to appear in a Cabernet Sauvignon flavour description?
slides.2.componentProps.items.13.explana: Cabernet Sauvignon typically shows blackcurrant, cedar/pencil shavings, and firm structure.
slides.2.componentProps.items.14.questio: Bordeaux city is located in which French administrative region?
slides.2.componentProps.items.14.explana: Bordeaux is the capital of Nouvelle-Aquitaine in south-west France and the capital of the Gironde department, in a temperate oceanic climate zone on the Atlantic coast.
slides.2.componentProps.items.15.questio: The typical flavour profile of Merlot is most closely described by which group?
slides.2.componentProps.items.15.explana: Merlot is known for its generous, round fruit — plum, blackberry, blueberry — and silky mouthfeel. More approachable than Cabernet Sauvignon, it is the dominant variety of the Right Bank.
slides.2.componentProps.items.16.questio: What was the main background that led to the 1855 Bordeaux Classification?
slides.2.componentProps.items.16.options: Napoleon III's request for the Paris World Exhibition
Bordeaux Chamber of Commerce self-initiated evaluation
slides.2.componentProps.items.16.explana: Napoleon III requested a classification to showcase Bordeaux's finest estates at the 1855 Paris Universal Exposition, completed by the Bordeaux Chamber of Commerce.
slides.2.componentProps.items.17.questio: What tier is Château d'Yquem in the Sauternes-Barsac classification?
slides.2.componentProps.items.17.explana: Château d'Yquem is the only Premier Cru Supérieur in the Sauternes-Barsac classification, outranking all other First Growths. It is widely considered one of the world's greatest sweet wines.
slides.2.componentProps.items.18.questio: What is the primary contribution of Sémillon in Bordeaux white wines?
slides.2.componentProps.items.18.explana: Sémillon's thin skin makes it susceptible to noble rot; in dry whites it contributes body, beeswax, and complex floral notes. With Sauvignon Blanc, it is key to both dry and sweet Bordeaux whites.
slides.2.componentProps.items.19.questio: What is the signature aroma profile of Cabernet Franc?
slides.2.componentProps.items.19.explana: Cabernet Franc typically shows violet, red berry, green/red pepper, and delicate pencil/graphite nuances, with softer tannins. It is an important component in Right Bank blends.
slides.2.componentProps.items.20.questio: What type of oak barrel do top Bordeaux red wines primarily use for ageing?
slides.2.componentProps.items.20.explana: Top Bordeaux châteaux predominantly use French oak (especially from Allier and Nevers forests), imparting subtle vanilla, spice, and tannin integration — more restrained and elegant than American oak.
slides.2.componentProps.items.21.questio: In which appellation is Château Pétrus located?
slides.2.componentProps.items.21.explana: Château Pétrus is Pomerol's flagship estate. Despite no official classification, its tiny production (~30,000 bottles/year), unique blue clay terroir, and exceptional quality make it one of Bordeaux's most expensive wines.
slides.2.componentProps.items.22.questio: Which of the following grape varieties does NOT belong to Bordeaux's approved varieties?
slides.2.componentProps.items.22.explana: Pinot Noir is Burgundy's signature variety and is neither grown nor permitted in Bordeaux. Bordeaux's approved red varieties include Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Malbec, Petit Verdot, and Carménère.
slides.2.componentProps.items.23.questio: In "Entre-Deux-Mers" (Between Two Seas), what do the "two seas" refer to?
slides.2.componentProps.items.23.options: The Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean
The Bay of Biscay and the English Channel
The north and south banks of the Gironde estuary
slides.2.componentProps.items.23.explana: "Entre-Deux-Mers" refers to the triangular land between the Garonne and Dordogne rivers, which converge north of Bordeaux to form the Gironde estuary. Known for dry white wines.
slides.2.componentProps.items.24.questio: What is the concept of a Bordeaux "Second Wine"?
slides.2.componentProps.items.24.options: A parallel product of identical quality
Made from batches not selected for the grand vin (younger vines or less-optimal plots)
A wine from a second-tier classified estate
A version with lower sulphite levels
slides.2.componentProps.items.24.explana: Second wines use grapes not selected for the grand vin — younger vines, less-optimal plots, or non-peak batches — offering the château's style at a more accessible price. Examples: Carruades de Lafite, Pavillon Rouge.
slides.2.componentProps.items.25.questio: The 1855 Classification divided Médoc red wines into how many tiers?
slides.2.componentProps.items.25.explana: The 1855 Classification divided Médoc reds (plus Haut-Brion from Graves) into five tiers (Premier Cru through Cinquième Cru), based on trading prices and reputation.
slides.2.componentProps.items.26.questio: What does "Mis en bouteille au Château" on a label indicate?
slides.2.componentProps.items.26.options: Aged at low temperature in the cellar
slides.2.componentProps.items.26.explana: "Mis en bouteille au Château" means "bottled at the château" — an important quality assurance indicating the wine was grown, made, and bottled entirely on the estate.
slides.2.componentProps.items.27.questio: In which year was the city of Bordeaux listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
slides.2.componentProps.items.27.explana: The historic centre of Bordeaux was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007, covering its historic architecture and port landscape.
slides.2.componentProps.items.28.questio: What does an AOC (Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée) designation mean to wine consumers?
slides.2.componentProps.items.28.options: Confirms origin, varieties, and production comply with regulatory controls
slides.2.componentProps.items.28.explana: AOC confirms the wine complies with specific geographic boundaries, permitted varieties, minimum alcohol levels, and production practices. It guarantees stylistic consistency but does not directly denote quality level.
slides.2.componentProps.items.29.questio: What does the word "Château" in the Bordeaux wine context actually mean?
slides.2.componentProps.items.29.options: An estate winery with its own vineyards, not necessarily a castle building
Must exceed 100 hectares to use the term
slides.2.componentProps.items.29.explana: In Bordeaux, "Château" broadly refers to an estate winery with its own vineyards — a castle building is not required. The term is used by estates of all sizes.
